claims.text: A hybrid Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulation can be applied to bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicitly modeling defects and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen will make conductivity predictions more accurate than traditional defect-free analytical models.
The claimed accuracy advantage applies in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Typically fabricated bulk HfNbTaTiZr contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed simulation explicitly represents point defects, extended defects, and oxygen distributions in the alloy lattice.
Oxygen impurities and other defects generate local lattice distortions and chemical disorder in HfNbTaTiZr.
Defect-induced lattice distortions and chemical disorder alter electron scattering.
Defect-induced lattice distortions and chemical disorder alter phonon interactions.
Representing non-ideal defect structures captures local variations in electronic scattering rates.
Representing non-ideal defect structures captures local variations in lattice dynamics.
Variations in electronic scattering control carrier mobility and electrical conductivity.
Conventional perfect-crystal analytical models cannot account for defect-induced scattering and lattice-distortion effects.
The hybrid simulation will reproduce experimental temperature-dependent conductivity trends more closely than ideal-crystal predictions.
Perfect-crystal analytical conductivity models typically deviate significantly from measurements on defect-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
The prediction is applicable only near the modeled oxygen concentration and within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Extrapolation to other alloy compositions, impurity levels, or temperature regimes may not be valid.
Hybrid MC/MD has previously been used to simulate nanostructure evolution in the related equimolar TaNbHfZr refractory alloy.
Prior hybrid MC/MD work on related refractory alloys has shown promise for electrical-conductivity prediction.
Failure to produce a statistically significant improvement over defect-free models across both temperature regimes would falsify the hypothesis.
